summary: Children aged 6–7 learn to compose 3-D shapes by stacking and combining real solids (cubes, prisms, cylinders, cones, spheres) into composite structures. The target skill is a progression: from unsystematic stacking, through trial-and-error assembly, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION — knowing in advance which shape will fit ('the cone goes on top') and naming a build by its component solids and their positions. Hands-on block-building with challenges pitched one level ahead, plus prompts to predict and describe, carries children forward; because this is a procedural, construction-based goal, physical block-building is the core medium. An on-screen 3-D sandbox is an optional supplementary model that preserves stacking, balance and depth, while flat drag-and-combine and matching tasks are useful scaffolds for naming parts but do not exercise balance or anticipation.
misconceptions: Adds blocks unsystematically and only recognises what it 'looks like' after building — no advance plan (a normal early trajectory level, not a fault).
Builds a composite but describes it only as one whole ('a rocket') and cannot name the component solids or their positions.
Places solids without regard to which faces are flat, so a cone or sphere used as a base makes the structure topple.

activities.title: Build a rocket with real solids
steps: Offer a set of real 3-D blocks: cubes, a cylinder, a cone, some prisms, and a sphere.
Ask the child to build a rocket by combining shapes so that it stands up.
Before each placement, prompt: 'Which shape will fit on top before you place it? Where will it go and why does it fit?'
After building, ask the child to point to and name each shape used and say where it sits (e.g. 'a cylinder at the bottom, a cone on top').

Try using the sphere as the base (or balancing the cone on its point) and let the child notice that it rolls or will not support more shapes, then choose a flat-faced solid — a cube, prism, or cylinder resting on a flat face — for the base.
activities.insight: A composite is made of named component solids combined on purpose; resting flat faces down keeps a structure stable, and you can plan which shape fits before placing it rather than only recognising the result afterwards.

activities.title: Challenges pitched one level ahead
steps: Watch how the child currently builds to judge their level (free stacking, trial-and-error assembly, or anticipating).
Set a building challenge just one step beyond that level — for example, from stacking identical cubes to combining a cone on a cylinder, or from trial-and-error assembly to predicting the next piece.
Scaffold with prompts and modelling, then gradually fade support as the child succeeds.
Repeat the same build and ask the child to say each shape as they add it.
activities.insight: Children advance most when the next task is just ahead of their current building, with support that fades, rather than jumping straight to the final target.

activities.title: On-screen 3-D building sandbox (optional)
steps: Drag 3-D solids into a build space and snap a cone onto a cylinder to make a rocket.
Try placing a sphere as a base; if the sandbox simulates gravity, watch whether it rolls and the tower falls, and talk about which faces must sit flat.
Before placing a piece, respond to the prompt 'which shape will fit on top?'
Tap the finished build to hear its component solids named in order ('cylinder… cone').
activities.insight: A 3-D model lets a child stack, combine and test balance, plan placements and have parts named — exercising the composing skill, including why a solid with no flat face, such as a sphere, makes a poor base.

activities.title: Match composites to their parts (naming activity)
steps: Show a picture or model of a composite (e.g. a cone-on-cylinder rocket, a cube tower, a house).
Ask the child to choose which component solids make it up and where each one sits.
Optionally use a reference image where tapping a part names it (rocket = cone + cylinder).
activities.insight: A composite can be decomposed into named component solids, each in a particular position — reinforcing part-naming vocabulary.

checkQuestion: Here are some 3-D blocks — cubes, a cylinder, a cone, some prisms. Build me a rocket by putting shapes together so it stands up. As you build, and when you finish, tell me which shapes you used and where each one is.
checkAnswer: Selects and stacks solids with anticipation to make the intended composite (e.g. a cylinder body with a cone on top), keeps it stable by resting flat faces down, and describes the result by naming its component solids and their positions ('a cylinder at the bottom, a cone on top').
